# What the future tells you about the present

# What the future tells you about the present

A walkthrough of the aciR package, from one function call to the point
where it refuses to answer

Published

2026-08-17

Abstract

Assimilative causal inference measures how much the later part of an
observed signal sharpens an estimate of something that was never
observed. This walkthrough climbs five rungs, from a single function
call on a two-variable system to a six-dimensional climate model, and
ends at the boundary where the package reports that the record ran out
before the question could be settled. Every number and figure below is
produced by running the code shown, on systems that are published and
cited.

The depth of the thermocline under the Pacific drives the sea-surface
temperatures that satellites record, and is itself far harder to
observe. That shape recurs everywhere: you have a signal you can
measure, and you want the state of something you cannot. This package
answers one narrow, answerable question about that pair. Given
everything the observed signal goes on to do *after* a given moment, how
much better can you say what the unobserved state was *at* that moment,
and how far ahead do you have to look before the answer stops improving?

Those are two different questions, and they get two different numbers.
What follows climbs from a single function call to the point where the
second question can no longer be answered from the record in hand, and
the package says so.

## 1 What this document is

Assimilative causal inference is a method for conditional Gaussian
nonlinear systems, published by Andreou et al. (2026). A conditional
Gaussian nonlinear system is one in which an observed signal evolves
nonlinearly, while the unobserved component, *conditional on the
observed path*, has Gaussian statistics available in closed form. That
closed form is what makes the method exact rather than approximate.

Two quantities follow from it. The **causal-information metric** is the
relative entropy, also called the Kullback-Leibler divergence, of the
smoother posterior from the filter posterior at each instant. In words:
how much the future of the observed record sharpens the estimate. The
**causal influence range** is the second quantity, and it asks how far
ahead one must look before that sharpening stops.

On the inputs The systems below are published mathematical models, and
the paths are simulated realisations of them or fixtures generated from
the reference implementation. **They are not observational records.** In
particular, the El Niño Southern Oscillation section uses a simulated
realisation of a published climate model, not measured sea-surface
temperatures, and nothing here supports an empirical claim about the
climate. The models, and the findings that use them, are in the source
paper.

Requirements `aciR` (0.2.3 or later), `ggplot2` and `DT`. Nothing is
downloaded: every fixture read below ships inside the installed package.
To install:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("biometryhub/ACI", subdir = "aciR")
```

## 2 Rung 1: the whole method in one call

Rung 1 of 5

The nonlinear dyad is the smallest system worth the trouble. One
observed variable, one unobserved variable, and a coupling that produces
intermittent bursts rather than steady behaviour. Those bursts are the
interesting part, because that is where the future of the observed
signal has the most to say.

`aci()` runs the whole workflow: the forward filter, the backward
smoother, and the metric that contrasts them.

``` r
model <- aci_dyad_model()
sim <- aci_simulate(model, n = 6000, seed = 42)
result <- aci(sim$x, model, dt = 0.001)

result
#> <aci> assimilative causal inference
#>   model: nonlinear dyad model with intermittent extreme events
#>   steps: 6000, dt: 0.001, time span: [0, 5.999]
#>   causal-information metric:
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> 0.00000 0.06639 0.11960 0.16478 0.20103 1.07480
```

The `print` method leads with the distribution of the metric rather than
a single number, because a single number would hide the thing that
matters: the metric is small most of the time and large in short
episodes.

``` r
d <- as.data.frame(result)

p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(t, x)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .32, colour = pal[1]) +
  labs(title = "The observed signal", y = "x", x = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(t, aci)) +
  geom_area(fill = pal[2], alpha = .22) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .38, colour = pal[2]) +
  labs(
    title = "What the future adds",
    subtitle = "Causal-information metric, in nats",
    y = "metric", x = "time"
  )

patch <- function(a, b) {
  gridExtra::grid.arrange(a, b, ncol = 1, heights = c(1, 1.15))
}
if (requireNamespace("gridExtra", quietly = TRUE)) {
  patch(p1, p2)
} else {
  print(p2)
}
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The metric peaks where the signal does something abrupt. That is the
substantive reading: during a burst, the record that arrives afterwards
carries a great deal of information about what the unobserved component
was doing at the time, and during quiet stretches it carries much less.

## 3 Rung 2: how far ahead must you look?

Rung 2 of 5

The metric says *how much*. It does not say *how long*. Two systems can
sharpen an estimate by the same total amount, one settling within a few
steps and the other still improving thousands of steps later. The causal
influence range separates them.

``` r
comp <- aci_dyad_components(sim$x, model$parameters)
filt <- aci_filter(sim$x, comp, dt = 0.001, mu0 = model$y0, R0 = 0.1)

cir <- aci_cir(
  sim$x, comp,
  dt = 0.001, filt = filt,
  window = seq(500L, 3000L, by = 250L)
)

cir
#> Causal influence range
#>   11 reported times, 0.499 to 2.999; 129 thresholds
#>   status: resolved 9  censored 2  below_threshold 0  insufficient 0
#>   objective range: median 0.1741 (0.075 to 0.2473)
#>   2 times are censored; those ranges are lower bounds
```

Two objective ranges are reported, and they differ here by more than a
factor of two. This is not a numerical disagreement. They are different
functionals that coincide only under a condition this system does not
meet.

``` r
cd <- as.data.frame(cir)
tbl(cd[, c("time", "objective", "objective_exact", "peak",
           "status", "monotone")])
```

Why the two ranges differ `objective_exact` averages the per-threshold
ranges over the whole threshold grid, which is the definition in the
source paper. `objective` is the efficient approximation the paper also
gives. They agree when the divergence sequence decreases with lag, by
the layer-cake identity. The `monotone` column reports that condition,
and here it is `FALSE` at every reported time, so the gap is
definitional rather than a defect in either. The package reports both
instead of picking one, because which is wanted depends on whether you
need the definition or the cheaper computation.

## 4 Rung 3: the question is not symmetric

Rung 3 of 5

Nothing so far distinguishes “what x says about y” from “what y says
about x”. A stochastic predator-prey system makes the asymmetry
concrete, because the same pair of populations can be read in either
causal direction. Observe the prey and infer the predator, or observe
the predator and infer the prey.

``` r
pp <- read.csv(ex("predprey_signal.csv"))
params <- aci_predprey_model()$parameters

run_direction <- function(direction) {
  observed <- if (direction == "predator_to_prey") pp$prey else pp$predator
  cmp <- aci_predprey_components(observed, params, direction)
  f <- aci_filter(observed, cmp, dt = 0.005, mu0 = 4, R0 = 0.1)
  s <- aci_smoother(observed, cmp, dt = 0.005, filt = f)
  data.frame(
    direction = direction,
    observed = if (direction == "predator_to_prey") "prey" else "predator",
    mean = mean(aci_metric(f, s)),
    peak = max(aci_metric(f, s)),
    drift_low = min(cmp$L_y),
    drift_high = max(cmp$L_y)
  )
}

both <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("predator_to_prey", "prey_to_predator"), run_direction
))
tbl(both)
```

The mean metric differs by roughly a factor of two between the two
readings of one system. Watching the predator tells you more about the
prey than the reverse, at these parameters.

This system also exercises something the dyad does not. The unobserved
component’s own drift coefficient is set by the observed state, so it
moves over the record and changes sign, shown by the `drift_low` and
`drift_high` columns. The latent process is damped at some times and
driven at others, which a system with a constant coefficient cannot
express.

## 5 Rung 4: six dimensions, and what one channel contributes

Rung 4 of 5

The El Niño Southern Oscillation model in the source paper is the
largest system the package expresses: six dimensions, three observed and
three unobserved, with coefficients that vary seasonally and noise
covariances that vary in time.

``` r
enso <- read.csv(ex("enso_signal.csv"))
p <- aci_enso_parameters()
emodel <- aci_enso_model(p)

c(observed = paste(emodel$observed, collapse = ", "),
  unobserved = paste(emodel$unobserved, collapse = ", "))
#>      observed    unobserved 
#> "T_C, T_E, I" "u, h_W, tau"
```

The observed channels are the central- and eastern-Pacific temperature
anomalies and the Walker circulation strength. The unobserved ones are
the zonal current, the thermocline depth and the wind burst.

``` r
ecomp <- aci_enso_components(
  enso$T_C, enso$T_E, enso$I, p = p, time = enso$t, dt = 0.005
)
xm <- rbind(enso$T_C, enso$T_E, enso$I)
mu0 <- c(6.9136e-04, -0.0028, -0.0256)
R0 <- 0.01 * diag(3L)

ef <- aci_filter(xm, ecomp, dt = 0.005, mu0 = mu0, R0 = R0)
es <- aci_smoother(xm, ecomp, dt = 0.005, filt = ef)
joint <- aci_metric(ef, es)

c(mean = mean(joint), peak = max(joint), at_time = enso$t[which.max(joint)])
#>       mean       peak    at_time 
#>  0.7817551  2.3470037 12.1400000
```

Six dimensions defeat the eye At three observed and three unobserved
dimensions there is no plot that settles whether this is right. A time
series of the metric can be shown, and is below, but it is orientation
rather than proof. What establishes the numbers is the parity grading
described at the end of this document, in which each quantity is
compared against the authors’ own code on the same input. Treat the
figure as a picture of the answer, not as evidence for it.

`aci_conditional()` asks a sharper question: what does one observed
channel contribute, when the others are still present in the system but
the filter stops assimilating them?

``` r
channels <- c("T_C", "T_E", "I")

contribution <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(channels), function(i) {
  cc <- aci_conditional(ecomp, target = i)
  f <- aci_filter(xm, cc, dt = 0.005, mu0 = mu0, R0 = R0)
  s <- aci_smoother(xm, cc, dt = 0.005, filt = f)
  m <- aci_metric(f, s)
  data.frame(channel = channels[i], mean = mean(m), peak = max(m))
}))
contribution <- rbind(
  contribution,
  data.frame(channel = "all three", mean = mean(joint), peak = max(joint))
)
tbl(contribution)
```

``` r
ggplot(
  data.frame(t = enso$t, metric = joint),
  aes(t, metric)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .34, colour = pal[3]) +
  labs(
    title = "Causal-information metric, six-dimensional model",
    subtitle = "Orientation only. The grading, not the picture, is the evidence.",
    x = "time", y = "metric (nats)"
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The central-Pacific channel on its own scores *higher* than all three
channels together, and the three parts sum to well over the whole. That
is the easiest result in this document to misread, so it is worth taking
apart rather than asserting an explanation for.

The tempting explanation is that a filter given fewer channels is worse,
which leaves the future more room to improve on it. That explanation is
wrong, and the package’s own output refutes it: restricted to the
central-Pacific channel, the *smoother’s* posterior widens by more than
the filter’s does, not less. Something else is moving.

Between two Gaussians the divergence splits into exactly two pieces. One
is the change in spread, how much narrower the smoother posterior is.
The other is the distance between the two posterior means, measured in
filter precisions. Computing both from the same filter and smoother the
package returns shows which one carries the metric.

``` r
kl_parts <- function(cmp) {
  f <- aci_filter(xm, cmp, dt = 0.005, mu0 = mu0, R0 = R0)
  s <- aci_smoother(xm, cmp, dt = 0.005, filt = f)
  n <- dim(f$cov)[3L]
  spread <- mean_shift <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    prec <- solve(f$cov[, , i])
    gap <- f$mean[, i] - s$mean[, i]
    spread[i] <- 0.5 * (sum(diag(prec %*% s$cov[, , i])) - 3 +
                          log(det(f$cov[, , i]) / det(s$cov[, , i])))
    mean_shift[i] <- 0.5 * as.numeric(t(gap) %*% prec %*% gap)
  }
  data.frame(spread = mean(spread), mean_shift = mean(mean_shift),
             total = mean(spread + mean_shift))
}

split <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list(ecomp, aci_conditional(ecomp, 1L), aci_conditional(ecomp, 2L),
       aci_conditional(ecomp, 3L)),
  kl_parts
))
split <- cbind(assimilating = c("all three", "T_C", "T_E", "I"), split)
split$mean_shift_pct <- round(100 * split$mean_shift / split$total)
tbl(split)
```

The `total` column reproduces the metric reported above, which is the
check that this decomposition is of the same quantity and not a
different one.

What the table shows Roughly three quarters of the metric is the
distance between the two posterior means, not the narrowing of the
posterior. Restricting to the central-Pacific channel leaves the spread
term essentially unchanged and raises the mean term. The metric
therefore reports mostly how far the future *moves* the estimate, and
only secondarily how much it *sharpens* it.

Two consequences follow, and they are the practical ones. The quantity
is not a decomposition, so per-channel values cannot be added and cannot
be read as a ranking of channel importance. And a channel scoring near
zero, as the Walker circulation does here on both terms, is saying that
its future neither moves nor sharpens the estimate beyond its own past.
That is not the same as the channel being uninformative about the
system.

The estimand is worth stating exactly, because four different quantities
get confused here. The metric is the relative entropy of
$`p(y_t \mid x_{0:T})`$ from $`p(y_t \mid x_{0:t})`$. It is not an
interventional quantity, not a Granger test and not transfer entropy,
although all four can be large at the same instants. Conditioning
changes what the filter assimilates, not the system that produced the
path.

## 6 Rung 5: where the package refuses

Rung 5 of 5

The binding constraint here is neither dimension nor runtime. It is how
much record remains *after* the moment you asked about. To find how far
ahead the influence reaches, the record has to reach at least that far,
and near the end of a record it does not.

This is a property of the question rather than of the software. No
method, in any language, can measure an influence extending further than
the data it was given, and an implementation that returned a confident
number there would be inventing it. What distinguishes implementations
is whether they report the shortfall or absorb it silently into a
plausible-looking value.

So the last rung is not a limitation being disclosed. It is the
behaviour worth checking for before trusting any of the previous four.
The same system is interrogated at thirty times, marching toward the end
of the record.

``` r
sim2 <- aci_simulate(model, n = 4000, seed = 7)
comp2 <- aci_dyad_components(sim2$x, model$parameters)
filt2 <- aci_filter(sim2$x, comp2, dt = 0.001, mu0 = model$y0, R0 = 0.1)

edge <- aci_cir(
  sim2$x, comp2,
  dt = 0.001, filt = filt2,
  window = seq(1000L, 3900L, by = 100L)
)

ed <- as.data.frame(edge)
ed$lookahead <- nrow(sim2) - ed$index
table(ed$status)
#> 
#> censored resolved 
#>       16       14
```

``` r
ggplot(ed, aes(lookahead, objective, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.1) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), linewidth = .3, colour = "#9aa5b1") +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(resolved = pal[3], censored = pal[2])) +
  labs(
    title = "The boundary is the record that remains, not the model",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Reading right to left, each point sits closer to the end of the record."
    ),
    x = "steps of record remaining after the reported time",
    y = "objective range"
  )
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The status changes from `resolved` to `censored` partway along. The rule
is explicit: a time is censored when the divergence has not settled
below `threshold` until it has consumed more than `1 - margin` of the
record available after it. At the default `margin = 0.1`, that means
more than 90%.

What the package does *not* do at that point is return `NA`. A censored
time still yields a statement the record supports, namely that the range
is at least this long, so the value stands and the status records that
it is a lower bound. Discarding it would throw away information exactly
at the end of the record, which is where somebody studying a recent
event is looking. Only a time with fewer than three later observations,
where no quadrature is possible at all, returns `NA`.

What to take from this rung A range reported near the end of a record is
a lower bound, and the `status` column is how you tell. Two habits
follow. Check `status` before quoting a range. And when you design a
record, leave more tail than the influence you expect to measure,
because the tail is the binding constraint.

## 7 How these numbers are checked

A reimplementation tested only against fixtures its own author
transcribed demonstrates self-consistency and nothing more. If the
author misread an equation, the fixture encodes the same misreading and
passes.

Every numerical claim in this package is therefore graded against a
source that did not also produce the code under test. The authors
publish their work as MATLAB scripts rather than as a callable library,
so their computational passages are lifted into callable functions as
byte-exact slices, never retyped, and a checker fails on a single byte
of drift. Both implementations then run on the same input and are
compared quantity by quantity.

``` r
tbl(data.frame(
  check = c(
    "Extract outputs reproducing the reference's own workspace",
    "Verbatim reference lines, none retyped",
    "Scalar core against the reference",
    "Predator-prey, both directions, filter through influence range"
  ),
  result = c(
    "156 of 156, difference exactly 0",
    "2,159 lines across 33 extracts",
    "26 of 26 quantities, worst 1.5e-14",
    "26 graded quantities, worst 1.5e-12"
  )
))
```

For scale, an experiment comparing independently developed
implementations of the same algorithms on identical input found
agreement degrading from six significant figures to one (Hatton, 1997).

The full record is in the [parity
ledger](https://biometryhub.github.io/ACI/ledgers/parity_ledger.md), and
the design history, with what remains open, is in the [development
ledger](https://biometryhub.github.io/ACI/ledgers/development_ledger.md).

## 8 Where to go next

``` r
tbl(data.frame(
  rung = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"),
  question = c(
    "How much does the future add?",
    "How far ahead must I look?",
    "Does the direction matter?",
    "What does one channel contribute?",
    "When should I not trust the answer?"
  ),
  entry_point = c(
    "aci()", "aci_cir()", "aci_predprey_components()",
    "aci_conditional()", "the status column of aci_cir()"
  )
))
```

Three articles ship with the package. *Assimilative causal inference on
the nonlinear dyad model* is the worked tutorial. *Assumptions and
interpretation* states the conditions under which the method applies and
what a peak does and does not support, and it is the right next read
after the two warnings above. *Validation and the independent oracle*
records what each oracle grades and, for each, what it does not.
